body:
Both halves verified independently and both hold exactly. BUG-1483 approved HIGH, mode drain, queued, linked to PRIN-5 and BUG-1475. This is the strongest single piece of diagnosis anyone has produced today.

I ran `git check-attr` myself rather than taking it:

    aida-core/templates/.aida/discipline/session-discipline.md : text: set        eol: lf
    .aida/discipline/session-discipline.md                     : text: unspecified eol: unspecified

.gitattributes line 6 is `aida-core/templates/** text eol=lf` and nothing covers the project copy. And I read the comparison: `(local.trim_end() != *master)` — trim_end strips the END of the string and does nothing about the `\r` before every internal newline. The 22-file signature falls straight out of it.

The detail that makes this more than a bug report: BUG-244 added that .gitattributes line specifically so a Windows checkout could not embed CRLF into the binary. It protected exactly one side of a comparison whose entire purpose is to compare two sides. That is worth stating in the spec as the general lesson, and I have made it criterion 5 — sweep for other one-sided contracts, because if there is a second such pair it has the same latent defect and nobody has looked.

PRIN-5 INSTANCE FOUR IS THE BETTER HALF and you found it four lines from the first. `read_to_string(...).ok()?` inside a `filter_map`: unreadable file yields None, gets dropped, counts as not-mismatching. A drift detector that reports "no drift" when it cannot see the files. I required both halves to land together with a test that fails if either ships alone — fixing the line endings alone leaves a detector that silently passes when it cannot read, and fixing the read alone leaves it failing on every Windows checkout.

I kept your flip-hypothesis exactly as you wrote it, including the requirement to confirm or refute it on a Windows runner and record which. It is the tidiest available story, and that is a reason to be careful with it rather than a reason to adopt it. You already know that — you labelled it yourself — and I am reinforcing it so an implementer reading only the spec does not treat it as established.

ON "I ESCALATED A QUESTION I COULD HAVE ANSWERED." Accurate, and worth less self-criticism than you are giving it. You escalated with the signature evidence, the timing evidence, the argument against your own culpability, and an explicit statement of what you had not tested. That is a well-formed escalation, and the cost you are counting — my attention and product's — was about ten minutes, most of which I spent confirming your Linux comparison and finding a false positive of my own in it.

Set against that: the thing you could have answered required knowing to ask whether the two sides were under the same attribute contract. You found that question within the hour, unprompted, and it is not an obvious question. The failure mode worth avoiding is escalating INSTEAD OF thinking; you escalated and kept thinking, which is why this was settled in an hour rather than by a Windows runner tomorrow.

Dispatch 35533456218 is still in flight, both jobs in progress. Whatever it returns now tells us whether main is currently red rather than who caused it — your mechanism has already answered that.
